answersA.title: Explain Go garbage collection
answersA.text: Garbage collection in Go is a concurrent, tri-color mark-and-sweep system. It automatically reclaims memory that is no longer in use by the program. This process happens in the background, minimizing pauses and allowing your application to continue running smoothly. The runtime manages this process, so you don't typically need to manually allocate or deallocate memory.

Indexes store a small representation of a collection's field or fields in a form that can be efficiently traversed, similar to how an index in a book helps you find information quickly. When you query a collection, MongoDB can use an index to locate the relevant documents much faster than scanning the entire collection. This is especially important for large datasets and frequently executed queries.

answersA.title: MongoDB indexing explained

When you query a collection, MongoDB can use the index to quickly locate the documents that match your query criteria, rather than having to examine every document in the collection. This significantly speeds up read operations, especially for large collections.

newInput: Explain the CAP theorem.

answersA.title: Explain the CAP theorem
answersA.text: The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide more than two out of the following three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Consistency means that every read receives the most recent write or an error. Availability means that every request receives a (non-error) response, without guarantee that it contains the most recent write. Partition tolerance means the system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped (or delayed) by the network between nodes. In practice, network partitions are inevitable, so systems must choose between Consistency and Availability when a partition occurs.

For example, a system might prioritize Consistency and Partition Tolerance (CP), sacrificing some Availability during a partition, or Availability and Partition Tolerance (AP), potentially serving stale data.

answersA.title: Eventual consistency explained
answersA.text: Eventual consistency is a consistency model in distributed systems. It guarantees that if no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses to that item will return the last updated value. This means that at any given moment, different nodes in a distributed system might have slightly different versions of the data, but these differences will resolve over time. It's a trade-off that prioritizes availability and partition tolerance over immediate consistency.

newInput: And how would you debounce a function?

answersA.text:
Debouncing a function is a technique to limit the rate at which a function can be called. It ensures that a function is only executed after a certain period of inactivity. This is commonly used for events like window resizing, scrolling, or user input to prevent excessive function calls.

To implement debouncing, you typically use a timer. When the debounced function is called, you clear any existing timer and set a new one. The actual function execution is then delayed until the timer expires without being cleared.

answersC.title: Define semaphore
answersC.text: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive that controls access to a shared resource by multiple processes or threads. It maintains a counter that is decremented when a process or thread requests access to the resource and incremented when it releases the resource. If the counter is zero when a request is made, the process or thread is blocked until the counter becomes positive. This prevents race conditions and ensures orderly access to the shared resource.

answersC.title: Définition du TDD
answersC.text: Le TDD, ou Test-Driven Development, est une méthodologie de développement logiciel. Elle consiste à écrire les tests automatisés avant d'écrire le code de production. Le cycle de développement suit généralement trois étapes : "Red" (écrire un test qui échoue), "Green" (écrire le code minimal pour faire passer le test) et "Refactor" (améliorer le code tout en maintenant les tests au vert). Cela permet de s'assurer que le code est bien testé et répond aux exigences dès le départ.

answersC.title: Qu'est-ce que le TDD ?
answersC.text: Le TDD signifie "Test-Driven Development", ou Développement piloté par les tests en français. C'est une méthodologie de développement logiciel où l'on écrit d'abord un test automatisé qui échoue, puis on écrit le code nécessaire pour que ce test réussisse. Enfin, on refactorise le code pour améliorer sa qualité tout en s'assurant que les tests continuent de passer. Ce cycle court, "rouge-vert-refactoriser", permet de concevoir un logiciel plus robuste et plus facile à maintenir.

newInput: Quelle est la différence entre une file et une pile ?

answersA.title: Différence entre file et pile
answersA.text: Une file est une structure de données qui suit le principe "premier entré, premier sorti" (FIFO), comme une file d'attente. Les éléments sont ajoutés à l'arrière (enqueue) et retirés de l'avant (dequeue). Une pile, en revanche, suit le principe "dernier entré, premier sorti" (LIFO), comme une pile d'assiettes. Les éléments sont ajoutés (push) et retirés (pop) du sommet.
